title: Israel's vote count: a deadlock
lines: Israel's vote count is almost complete, and the result is a deadlock.
With about ninety percent of votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc has fifty-three seats, according to the Times of Israel and Ynet.
Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc has forty-eight. A government needs sixty-one of the Knesset's one hundred and twenty seats.
Likud is still the largest single party, with twenty-six seats. Eisenkot's Yashar has twenty-one, and Naftali Bennett's party twelve.
The big story is the Arab parties. Together, the Joint List and Ra'am have nineteen seats, their highest ever, on record turnout in Arab towns.
Netanyahu claimed that high Arab turnout was part of an effort to steal the election. The Central Elections Committee said it had seen no sign of systematic tampering.
Eisenkot said the public chose change, and called on Netanyahu to step down. Netanyahu urged what he called the Zionist majority to unite.
The Joint List says it is ready to help remove Netanyahu's government. But most Zionist parties have ruled out working with the Arab parties.
About half a million special ballots, mostly from soldiers, are still being counted. Each seat is worth about forty thousand votes, so a few seats could still change.
Official final results are due on the fourth of November. Analysts see three options: a deal involving Arab parties, a unity government, or another election.
Until a new government is formed, Netanyahu's current government stays in office as a caretaker.
